panels.text: Daniel Kahneman once taught flight instructors that praise works better than punishment for building skill.
A veteran instructor objected. Cadets he praised for a clean manoeuvre usually did worse next time. Cadets he screamed at usually did better.
Kahneman saw the catch. A very good (or very bad) attempt is partly luck, and luck rarely repeats, so the next attempt tends to land nearer the average. This is regression to the mean.
The twist: we tend to praise the good and scold the bad, so it can look as if praise backfires and scolding helps. The same effect gives sport its "sophomore slump" after a great rookie season.

probes.question: A cadet's best-ever flight is followed by a weaker one. What is the most likely reason?
options: Exceptional results include luck, which rarely repeats

probes.question: A great rookie season followed by a worse second year is called the sophomore ____.

claims.claim: Kahneman taught flight instructors that praise works better than punishment for building skill
claims.quote: attempting to teach flight instructors that praise is more effective than punishment for promoting skill-learning
claims.note: Page says 'attempting to teach'; card 'once taught' is a fair paraphrase.

claims.claim: Veteran instructor: praised cadets usually did worse next time, screamed-at cadets usually did better
claims.quote: I have often screamed at cadets for bad execution, and in general they do better the next time

claims.claim: Exceptional attempts include luck, which rarely repeats, so next attempt lands nearer average (regression to the mean)
claims.quote: Hence, those who did well previously are unlikely to do quite as well in the second test

claims.claim: We praise the good and scold the bad, so it can seem praise backfires and scolding helps
claims.quote: regression to the mean might explain why rebukes can seem to improve performance, while praise seems to backfire

claims.claim: Great rookie season followed by worse second year is the sophomore slump (probe cloze)
claims.quote: Baseball players who hit well in their rookie season are likely to do worse their second
claims.note: Page names it the "sophomore slump" in the same passage.
